raw_findings.message: The ID depends only on customer and date, so every invoice for the same customer on the same date receives the same identifier, making distinct invoices indistinguishable.
SKU and description text is inserted into the rendered invoice without escaping newlines, so crafted item data can inject forged invoice lines or totals.
The displayed tax is calculated on the subtotal even though the invoice total uses tax on the discounted net amount, so invoices with a discount show inconsistent figures.
The output path is concatenated into a shell command, so a path containing shell metacharacters can execute attacker-chosen commands when `--out` is used.
The check accepts positive infinity because it only rejects negative prices, so a JSON value such as `1e400` can produce invalid infinite invoice amounts.
Any negative integer quantity is accepted, allowing input items to subtract from the subtotal and produce incorrect invoice totals.
Invalid entries are silently discarded, so a malformed line item can be omitted from an otherwise successful invoice without warning.
Subtotal accumulation uses binary floating-point arithmetic without cent rounding, so values such as three one-cent-unit entries priced at 0.10 can produce an inaccurate subtotal.
Discount percentages are not constrained to the range 0–100, so a discount above 100 can make the invoice total negative.
Tax is floored rather than rounded to cents, so 10% tax on 19.99 is charged as 1.99 instead of 2.00.
The effective tax rate divides by the net amount without handling zero, so a full discount or zero-value invoice prints `NaN` or infinity.
The final page's last-item index is not capped at the item count, so invoices with more than ten items and a partial final page access `undefined` and crash while rendering.
The script unconditionally opens `DEFECTS.json`, which is absent from the project, so it raises an error after running the cases instead of completing as documented.

The supplied date is never checked against the documented `YYYY-MM-DD` format, so inputs such as `not-a-date` are printed and used to create invoice IDs.
Untrusted customer and item text is rendered without escaping control characters, so embedded newlines or ANSI sequences can forge invoice output or manipulate a terminal.

The price check accepts non-finite values, so a JSON value such as `1e400` becomes `Infinity` and produces invalid monetary totals.
`Number.isInteger` also accepts integers outside JavaScript’s safe-integer range, so a large quantity can make line totals and subtotals imprecise.
The script unconditionally opens `DEFECTS.json`, which is absent from the project, so `repro.sh` fails with a file-not-found error after running its cases.

raw_findings.message: The identifier depends only on customer and date, so separate invoices for the same customer on the same date receive the same invoice number.
A SKU or description containing newlines is inserted verbatim into the text invoice, allowing input to add forged invoice rows or totals.
The rendered tax line is calculated from the subtotal rather than the discounted net amount, so it disagrees with the tax and total actually computed when a discount is applied.
The output path is concatenated into a shell command, so a path containing shell metacharacters can execute attacker-chosen commands when `--out` is used.
The check accepts positive infinity, which can be produced by a JSON number such as `1e999` and then yields invalid totals or `null` values in JSON output.
Any integer quantity is accepted, including negative quantities, allowing input to reduce the subtotal with fictitious returns.
Invalid item entries are swallowed and omitted from the invoice, so malformed input can produce a successful invoice that silently excludes requested items.
Subtotal accumulation uses binary floating-point arithmetic, so valid amounts such as three items priced at 0.10 can produce an inaccurate JSON subtotal of 0.30000000000000004.
Discounts are not restricted to the 0–100 percent range, so values over 100 produce negative net amounts and totals, while negative values act as surcharges.
Tax is floored rather than rounded to the nearest cent, so 10% tax on 19.99 is reported as 1.99 instead of 2.00.
When the net amount is zero, this divides zero tax by zero and displays `NaN` as the effective tax rate.
For a final page with fewer than `perPage` items, `last` is undefined and accessing `last.sku` crashes invoice rendering.
Running the documented reproduction script fails when it tries to open `DEFECTS.json`, which is not present among the project files.

fixed_raw_findings.message: SKU and description (and the customer field on line 72) are interpolated into invoice text without escaping, so input containing newlines or terminal control sequences can forge invoice lines or manipulate terminal output.
All page footers are appended after the totals rather than at their page breaks, so invoices with more than ten items do not actually show a footer on each printed page.
The price check accepts values such as JSON `1e400` as `Infinity`, which then produces `NaN` or infinite invoice totals; reject non-finite and out-of-range values before doing cent arithmetic.
Converting decimal prices to cents with binary floating-point can misround values such as `1.005` to 100 cents instead of 101, producing an incorrect invoice amount.
The script unconditionally opens `DEFECTS.json`, which is absent from the project, so `repro.sh` fails after running its cases instead of completing as documented.

raw_findings.message: The `--date` value is never validated, so values outside the documented `YYYY-MM-DD` format or impossible dates are printed on invoices and used to derive their IDs.
The ID depends only on customer and date, so distinct invoices for the same customer on the same date receive the same identifier.
Customer names and item text are inserted into the text invoice without escaping, so embedded newlines or terminal control characters can forge or obscure invoice content.
The displayed tax is calculated on the subtotal while the total uses tax on the discounted net amount, so invoices with a discount show a tax line inconsistent with their total.
All page footers are appended after the entire invoice rather than placed at their respective page boundaries, so multi-page invoices do not have per-page footers.
The output path is concatenated into a shell command, so a path such as `inv.txt;touch pwned.flag` executes attacker-controlled commands when `--out` is used.
The parser accepts non-finite unit prices because it checks only the type and lower bound, so a JSON value such as `1e400` can produce infinite invoice amounts.
The parser checks that quantity is an integer but not that it is non-negative, so negative quantities can reduce the subtotal and produce invalid invoices.
Invalid items are discarded without reporting an error, so a malformed line item can disappear from an otherwise successful invoice and its totals.
The discount is checked only for finiteness, so negative discounts or discounts above 100 percent are accepted and can produce surcharges or negative totals.
Money is accumulated using binary floating-point values, so inputs such as three items priced at `0.1` can yield inaccurate totals and expose artifacts in JSON output.
Tax is floored to cents rather than rounded, so a tax amount such as 10% of 19.99 is reported as 1.99 instead of 2.00.
The effective tax rate divides by the net amount without handling zero, so a full discount or zero-value invoice prints `NaN`.
For a final page with fewer than `perPage` items, the indexed last item is undefined and accessing its SKU throws, so invoices with 11–19 items fail to render.

For invoices with more than ten items, all page footer strings are appended after the totals instead of being placed at their corresponding page boundaries.
